$comment: AWS Secrets Manager — the first G4 wave-2 service (docs/plans/compat-coverage-modelgen.md §5). Unlike wave 1, Overcast implements this one: 19 of the model's 23 operations carry a capability row other than Unsupported, so these groups produce real pass/fail rather than the uniform `unimplemented`/`skip` of a Tier-0 recipe. Four things shape the file. (1) The delete is forced. AWS's DeleteSecret schedules deletion behind a recovery window of at least 7 days by default, and a scheduled secret still answers DescribeSecret — with a DeletedDate — so absence after delete would be false against real AWS. ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery skips the window, and DescribeSecret then raises the ResourceNotFoundException the derived absence check wants. The other half of that choice is `async`: AWS documents the forced delete as performed "with an asynchronous background process, so there might be a short delay before the secret is permanently deleted", which is exactly the consistency window `async` exists to poll over. (2) There is no ListTagsForResource. Secrets Manager returns a secret's tags on DescribeSecret, so that is the tag listing, and the generator folds the listing's own test into the read it already has. (3) A version is its own resource. PutSecretValue creates one, GetSecretValue by VersionId reads it back, ListSecretVersionIds lists it, and UpdateSecretVersionStage attaches a custom staging label the read-back then fetches by — the shape AWS's own UpdateSecretVersionStage example uses. A version has no delete operation on AWS ("You can't directly delete a version of a secret"), so the resource declares none and the group's teardown removes the secret that holds it. (4) The resource-policy quartet is authored rather than derived: ValidateResourcePolicy, PutResourcePolicy, GetResourcePolicy and DeleteResourcePolicy are a write/read/absence chain over one document, and the document is the one AWS's own ValidateResourcePolicy example sends. Two implemented operations are deliberately left uncovered rather than guessed at, and both are recorded in gaps.json as probe-of-implemented-op: RotateSecret needs a rotation Lambda ARN — AWS answers InvalidRequestException for "a secret that doesn't already have a Lambda function ARN configured" when the call supplies none — and a compat run owns no Lambda, because the corpus has no cross-service resources. RestoreSecret would be the natural partner to a scheduled delete and is Unsupported here, so the scheduled-deletion path has no read that could prove it either way.

neverProbe.RemoveRegionsFromReplication: Deletes a secret's replicas in other Regions. AWS deletes a replica immediately — there is no recovery window for one — so the secret value stops being readable in that Region the moment the call lands, and nothing in a probe group puts it back.
neverProbe.ReplicateSecretToRegions: Creates a copy of the secret in other Regions. Each replica is a separate billed secret that outlives the run, and ForceOverwriteReplicaSecret will overwrite a secret somebody already keeps under that name in the destination Region.
neverProbe.RestoreSecret: Cancels a scheduled deletion. Aimed at a stranger's secret it un-deletes something the owner deliberately scheduled for removal, and the recovery window is the only notice that owner gets before the secret goes for good.
neverProbe.StopReplicationToReplica: Promotes a replica to a standalone secret and breaks its link to the primary. The split is not reversible — the two secrets diverge from that call onwards — and it is run against the replica, which is somebody's live secret.

resources.$comment: The secret itself. Identity is the ARN: CreateSecret returns it, DescribeSecret repeats it, and ListSecrets carries it on every entry, so one export serves the read-back, the list-membership check and every authored clause. The description is not in `create.params`: `mutable.from` is merged into the create, so the create's own read-back asserts the initial value and UpdateSecret is a real change rather than a rewrite of the same string. Three of its fields need explaining. `tags.list` is DescribeSecret because Secrets Manager has no ListTagsForResource — a secret's tags come back on the describe — and since DescribeSecret already carries the read test the generator folds the listing's own test into it and says so in the review report; the tag and untag tests still verify through a DescribeSecret call of their own. `delete` is forced because the derived absence check is a not-found on that read, and AWS's default delete leaves DescribeSecret answering for the whole of a recovery window of at least seven days; RecoveryWindowInDays and ForceDeleteWithoutRecovery may not both be sent, so the forced form sends neither window. `async` is ten seconds of budget for the one delay AWS documents here: "Secrets Manager performs the actual deletion with an asynchronous background process, so there might be a short delay before the secret is permanently deleted."

list.$comment: ListSecrets is account-wide and its @paginated trait names no items member, so itemsPath is derived from the output's sole top-level list. The name filter is what keeps the check bounded: AWS documents the `name` key as a case-sensitive prefix match, and the value here is the whole name, so exactly one entry can match however many secrets the account already holds. Without it a run sharing an emulator with other groups would be asserting membership of whatever fits on one page.

operations.$comment: The one operation here that touches no secret. It is in this group rather than a probe because GetRandomPassword is implemented, and an implemented operation may not be probed. The assertion is the whole of what the request asked for: exactly twenty-four characters, and no punctuation, which is what ExcludePunctuation means with IncludeSpace left off.

The batch read, scoped to the one secret this group owns. Membership is by ARN and by the value the create wrote, so the entry has to be this secret and has to carry its content — a batch that answered with the right ARN and an empty value would fail.

The policy document is the one AWS's own ValidateResourcePolicy example sends, whitespace removed: a single account root as the principal, which is what makes it pass the wide-access check the operation exists to run. SecretId is optional on this operation and is sent because AWS's example sends it.

The read-back matches rather than equals: AWS is not documented to return the policy byte-for-byte as it was sent, and the thing worth asserting is that the stored document is the one this test put there. The action string appears nowhere else in the response.
Its own test after the put above, so the operation is exercised as a read rather than only as somebody else's read-back.
Absence of the member, not an empty string: AWS returns only the fields that have a value, so a secret with no resource policy answers GetResourcePolicy with ARN and Name alone.

Rotation was never turned on for this secret, and AWS's documented InvalidRequestException causes for this operation do not include that case — the one rotation cause listed is about *enabling* rotation without a Lambda ARN. So the call is expected to succeed and the assertion is the identity it answers with. RotationEnabled is deliberately not asserted: AWS returns null for it when a secret has never been configured for rotation, so neither true nor false nor missing is a value a scenario could hold both AWS and an emulator to.

resources.$comment: A second version of the secret. PutSecretValue is the create, and with VersionStages left out AWS moves AWSCURRENT onto the new version — which is why the read fetches by VersionId rather than by stage: it must name this version whatever the labels are doing. There is no DeleteSecretVersion on AWS ("You can't directly delete a version of a secret"; a version is deprecated by losing its last staging label and collected later), so the resource declares no delete and the group's teardown removes the secret that holds it. No `async` here: AWS documents a consistency window for the forced delete and for nothing else in this service.

list.$comment: ListSecretVersionIds carries no @paginated items member either, so itemsPath is derived from the sole top-level list. The listing is scoped to this secret by SecretId, so membership by version id is exact.

operations.$comment: Attaching a staging label that is attached nowhere else, which AWS's own first example for this operation does with only MoveToVersionId — RemoveFromVersionId is required only when the label already sits on another version. The read-back is what makes the label observable: GetSecretValue addressed by stage has to come back with this version's id and the value the create wrote, which is a stronger statement than the operation's own response (ARN and Name) can make.
